questions.q: What is the basic economic problem?
questions.why: Scarcity forces choices about what to produce, how and for whom.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is…
o: the money price of a good
the next best alternative given up
questions.why: Choosing one option means losing the benefit of the next best.

questions.q: A shift outwards of a production possibility curve shows…
questions.why: More or better resources let the economy produce more of both goods.

questions.q: A farmer uses a tractor to plough a field. Which factor of production is the tractor?
questions.why: Capital is a man-made good used to produce other goods and services.

questions.q: Sara spends $20 on a book. Her next choice would have been a cinema ticket, and her third choice a meal. What is the opportunity cost of the book?
questions.why: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative given up, which is the cinema ticket.

long.q: Define opportunity cost and explain, using an example, the opportunity cost a government faces when it decides to spend more on healthcare.
scheme: B1: opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
B1: the government's resources (tax revenue) are scarce, so spending more on healthcare means less can be spent elsewhere
B1: example: the next best use given up, e.g. new schools or roads that cannot now be built

long.q: Identify the four factors of production and state the reward to each.
scheme: B1: land: rent
B1: labour: wages
B1: capital: interest
B1: enterprise: profit

long.q: An economy can produce these combinations of food and machines: A 100 food and 0 machines; B 90 food and 10 machines; C 70 food and 20 machines; D 40 food and 30 machines. Calculate the opportunity cost of increasing the output of machines from 10 to 20, and from 20 to 30, and explain why it changes.
scheme: B1: from 10 to 20 machines: 20 units of food given up (2 food per machine)
B1: from 20 to 30 machines: 30 units of food given up (3 food per machine)
B1: the opportunity cost rises as more machines are made
B1: because resources are not equally suited to both goods: the resources moved later are better at making food than machines

long.q: Explain two causes of an outward shift of a country's production possibility curve.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. an increase in the quantity of resources (more workers through immigration, more capital through investment)
B1: explained: the economy can produce more of both goods, so the maximum output rises
B1: a second cause, e.g. an improvement in the quality of resources (education and training, better technology)
B1: explained: each resource becomes more productive

long.q: Explain the difference between an economic good and a free good, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: an economic good is scarce: making it uses resources, so it has an opportunity cost
B1: example, e.g. a car / a loaf of bread
B1: a free good is not scarce: it needs no resources to make, so there is no opportunity cost
B1: example, e.g. air / sea water / sunlight

questions.q: If the price of a good rises, what happens to the quantity demanded?
questions.why: A movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

questions.q: Which causes the demand curve for tea to shift right?
o: A fall in the price of tea
A rise in the price of coffee (a substitute)
A rise in the price of tea
questions.why: A dearer substitute makes people switch to tea at every price.

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand is −0.5. Demand is…
questions.why: Its value is less than 1 (ignoring the sign), so quantity changes less than price.

questions.q: A maximum price set below the equilibrium price causes…
questions.why: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the lower price.

questions.q: A merit good is…
o: beneficial and underconsumed in a free market
questions.why: Examples are education and healthcare; people underestimate their benefits.

questions.q: A government sets a maximum price on bread. Where must it be set to have an effect?
o: Anywhere, it always has an effect
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many shifted a curve to show a lower equilibrium instead of drawing a maximum price line below equilibrium.

long.q: Explain two factors that could cause the supply of a product to increase.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. lower costs of production (raw materials, wages)
B1: explained: more profitable to produce at each price, so the supply curve shifts right
B1: a second factor, e.g. improved technology / a subsidy / good weather
B1: explained with its effect on supply

long.q: The price of a good falls from $5 to $4 and the quantity demanded rises from 100 to 130 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity = +30%, % change in price = −20%
B1: elastic (greater than 1, ignoring the sign)

long.q: Explain what happens in a free market when the price is above the equilibrium price.
scheme: B1: at that price quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
B1: so there is excess supply (a surplus) and unsold goods build up
B1: sellers cut their price to sell their stock
B1: quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls until equilibrium is reached

long.q: The price of a good rises from $8 to $10 and the quantity supplied rises from 400 to 460 units. Calculate the price elasticity of supply, state whether supply is elastic or inelastic, and explain one factor that could make supply more elastic.
scheme: M1: % change in quantity supplied = 60 ÷ 400 × 100 = 15%; % change in price = 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25%
B1: inelastic (less than 1)
B1: a factor, e.g. spare capacity / large inventories / a longer time period / resources easily moved between uses

long.q: Explain why a free market may under-provide a merit good such as education, and one way a government could correct this.
scheme: B1: consumers underestimate the benefits to themselves (lack of information)
B1: and ignore the external benefits to others, e.g. a more productive workforce
B1: so demand and consumption are below the socially best level
B1: a correction, e.g. provide it free through state schools / subsidise it / make it compulsory / give information

questions.q: What is the main function of a central bank?
o: Issuing currency and setting interest rates
questions.why: It controls monetary policy and acts as the government's and banks' bank.

questions.q: Division of labour means…
questions.why: Specialisation raises productivity but can make work repetitive.

questions.q: Total revenue is…
questions.why: Profit = total revenue − total cost.

questions.q: As a supermarket chain grows, it buys goods in bulk at a lower price per unit. This is an example of…
questions.why: Bulk buying lowers average cost because of the firm's own growth, so it is an internal purchasing economy of scale.

questions.q: A firm produces 200 units. Its fixed costs are $1 000 and its total variable costs are $600. What is its average total cost?
questions.why: Average total cost = total cost ÷ output = (1 000 + 600) ÷ 200 = $8.

long.q: A firm has fixed costs of $600. It makes 150 units with total variable costs of $900 and sells each unit for $12. Calculate its total cost, its average total cost and its profit.
scheme: B1: average total cost = 1500 ÷ 150 = $10
M1: total revenue = 150 × 12 = $1800

long.q: Explain two reasons why some workers earn more than others.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. differences in skills, qualifications and training
B1: explained, e.g. skilled workers are scarce (low supply) and more productive, so firms pay more
B1: a second reason, e.g. demand for the product they make / trade union strength / discrimination / working conditions / public or private sector
B1: explained with its effect on demand for or supply of the labour

long.q: Explain two factors that influence how much a household saves.
scheme: B1: one factor, e.g. the level of income
B1: explained, e.g. higher-income households can save more after paying for necessities
B1: a second factor, e.g. the rate of interest / confidence about the future / age / availability of saving schemes
B1: explained, e.g. a higher interest rate rewards saving, so households save more

long.q: Discuss whether a monopoly is always bad for consumers.
scheme: B1: a reason it may be bad, e.g. higher prices because there are no close substitutes
B1: explained, e.g. the monopolist restricts output to raise price and profit
B1: a second disadvantage, e.g. less choice / lower quality / less pressure to be efficient
B1: a reason it may be good, e.g. economies of scale can lower average costs and prices
B1: a second advantage, e.g. high profits fund research and new products / avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly)
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. depends on whether it is regulated and whether cost savings are passed on

long.q: Apart from buying in bulk, explain two internal economies of scale that a large car manufacturer could benefit from.
scheme: B1: one economy, e.g. technical: using large, specialised machinery and production lines
B1: explained: the cost of the machinery is spread over many cars, so the average cost falls
B1: a second economy, e.g. financial (borrowing at lower interest) / managerial (specialist managers) / marketing (advertising cost spread over more sales) / risk-bearing
B1: explained with how it lowers average cost

questions.q: Which is a macroeconomic aim of government?
questions.why: Aims include growth, low unemployment, stable prices, a sustainable balance of payments and fair income distribution.

questions.q: A progressive tax…
o: takes the same percentage from everyone
takes a larger percentage from higher incomes
takes a smaller percentage from higher incomes
questions.why: Income tax with rising rates is an example.

questions.q: Inflation is measured in many countries using…
questions.why: A CPI tracks the price of a weighted basket of goods and services.

questions.q: Cutting interest rates is likely to…
questions.why: Cheaper borrowing encourages consumption and investment.

questions.q: A consumer price index rises from 120 to 126 over a year. What is the rate of inflation?
questions.why: Inflation = change ÷ original index × 100 = 6 ÷ 120 × 100 = 5%.

long.q: Explain two causes of unemployment.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. cyclical: a fall in aggregate demand in a recession
B1: explained: firms produce less, so need fewer workers
B1: a second cause, e.g. structural: decline of an industry / skills mismatch, or frictional
B1: explained with how it creates unemployment

long.q: A country's consumer price index has two groups of items: food, with a weight of 60, and transport, with a weight of 40. In a year food prices rise by 5% and transport prices by 10%. Calculate the rate of inflation and explain one reason why it may not reflect the experience of every household.
scheme: M1: weighted changes: 0.6 × 5 = 3 and 0.4 × 10 = 4
M1: add the weighted changes
A1: inflation = 7%
B1: households spend in different proportions from the weights, e.g. a family without a car spends little on transport

long.q: A country's labour force is 20 million and 1.2 million people are unemployed. Calculate the unemployment rate and explain two costs of unemployment to the economy.
scheme: B1: one cost, e.g. lost output: the economy produces inside its production possibility curve
B1: a second cost, e.g. the government receives less tax and spends more on benefits / skills are lost / social problems

long.q: Discuss whether cutting income tax is the best way for a government to increase economic growth.
scheme: B1: lower income tax raises disposable income, so consumer spending and aggregate demand rise
B1: it may also increase incentives to work and to set up businesses, raising productive capacity
B1: a limit, e.g. people may save the extra income or spend it on imports
B1: a further limit, e.g. lower tax revenue means less government spending or more borrowing; may cause inflation
B1: an alternative, e.g. lower interest rates, more spending on education and infrastructure, or other supply-side policies
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. depends on whether there is spare capacity and on the cause of slow growth

long.q: Explain two supply-side policy measures a government could use to reduce unemployment.
scheme: B1: one measure, e.g. more spending on education and training
B1: explained: workers gain the skills employers need, reducing structural unemployment
B1: a second measure, e.g. better information on job vacancies / lower taxes on firms / reduced benefits to increase incentives / deregulation
B1: explained: e.g. job-seekers find work faster, reducing frictional unemployment

questions.q: Which indicator combines income, education and life expectancy?
questions.why: The Human Development Index measures more than income.

questions.q: Absolute poverty means…
o: not having enough for basic needs
questions.why: Relative poverty compares income with others in the country.

questions.q: Why does the size of a country's population not change its death rate directly?
o: Death rate is measured per 1000 of the population
Death rate is a total number
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common error was to cite population size; death rate is per 1000 people, so size cancels out.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 30 per 1000 and a death rate of 10 per 1000, with no migration. What is its rate of natural increase?
questions.why: Natural increase = 30 − 10 = 20 per 1000, which is 2% of the population a year.

questions.q: Compared with a developed economy, which is most likely to be a feature of a developing economy?
o: A larger share of workers in the primary sector
A higher proportion of elderly people
questions.why: Developing economies usually rely more on agriculture and mining, while developed ones have more tertiary-sector jobs.

long.q: Explain why real GDP per head may not be a good measure of living standards in a country.
scheme: B1: it is an average, so it ignores how income is distributed: many people may be poor
B1: it does not measure the quality of life, e.g. health, education, pollution or working hours
B1: it leaves out output that is not traded, e.g. subsistence farming or the informal economy
B1: it does not show what the output is, e.g. high spending on weapons rather than consumer goods

long.q: A country has a population of 50 million, a birth rate of 24 per 1000 and a death rate of 9 per 1000. Net migration is −50 000 a year. Calculate the change in its population over one year.
scheme: M1: natural increase rate = 24 − 9 = 15 per 1000
A1: population change = 750 000 − 50 000 = +700 000

long.q: Explain two causes of poverty in a developing economy.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. unemployment and underemployment / low wages
B1: explained, e.g. people have little or no income to buy basic necessities
B1: a second cause, e.g. poor education and health care / low productivity / high population growth / poor infrastructure / corruption or conflict
B1: explained with how it keeps incomes low

long.q: Explain two consequences of an ageing population for an economy.
scheme: B1: one consequence, e.g. government spending on pensions and healthcare rises
B1: explained, e.g. taxes may need to rise or other spending be cut
B1: a second consequence, e.g. a smaller labour force / higher dependency ratio / changes in demand towards goods for older people
B1: explained, e.g. fewer workers may mean labour shortages and slower growth

long.q: Discuss whether foreign aid is the best way to reduce poverty in a developing economy.
scheme: B1: aid can pay for schools, hospitals, clean water and infrastructure
B1: explained, e.g. this raises productivity and incomes in the long run
B1: a limitation, e.g. aid may be wasted through corruption / tied to buying the donor's goods / creates dependency
B1: an alternative, e.g. trade, foreign direct investment, microfinance, government policies on education or minimum wages
B1: explained with its effect on poverty
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. aid is most useful when well targeted and combined with other policies

questions.q: A tariff is…
questions.why: Quotas limit quantity; tariffs raise import prices.

questions.q: If a country's currency depreciates, its exports become…
questions.why: Foreign buyers need less of their currency to buy the same goods.

questions.q: A current account deficit means…
o: exports of goods and services exceed imports
imports of goods and services exceed exports
questions.why: The current account mainly records trade in goods and services plus income flows.

questions.q: What is the opportunity cost of a firm exporting its goods?
o: Selling those goods on the home market
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a number thought the opportunity cost of exporting is importing. It is the next best alternative: selling at home.

questions.q: Why might a government impose a quota on imported steel?
o: To lower steel prices for consumers
To raise tax revenue from imports
To protect domestic steel producers and jobs
To increase the variety of steel available
questions.why: A quota limits the quantity of imports, reducing competition for domestic producers; unlike a tariff it raises no tax revenue, and prices tend to rise.

long.q: Explain two benefits of free trade for a country.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. countries specialise where they have a comparative advantage
B1: explained: more output overall, lower costs and prices
B1: a second benefit, e.g. more choice for consumers / bigger markets for firms / competition raising efficiency
B1: explained

long.q: A country's exports of goods are $40 billion and imports of goods $52 billion. Exports of services are $18 billion and imports of services $9 billion. Net primary income is −$3 billion and net secondary income is +$2 billion. Calculate the balance on the current account.
scheme: M1: trade in goods balance = 40 − 52 = −$12 billion
M1: trade in services balance = 18 − 9 = +$9 billion
M1: add net primary and secondary income: −12 + 9 − 3 + 2
A1: current account = −$4 billion (a deficit)

long.q: Explain two causes of a depreciation of a country's floating exchange rate.
scheme: B1: one cause, e.g. a fall in demand for the country's exports
B1: explained: foreigners need less of the currency, so demand for it falls
B1: a second cause, e.g. a cut in interest rates / more imports bought / speculation / higher inflation than abroad
B1: explained, e.g. lower interest rates make saving there less attractive, so hot money flows out and the supply of the currency rises

long.q: Discuss whether a government should impose tariffs to protect its domestic steel industry.
scheme: B1: a reason for, e.g. protects jobs in the steel industry
B1: a second reason, e.g. protects a strategic industry / stops dumping / raises tax revenue / reduces a current account deficit
B1: a reason against, e.g. higher prices for steel users such as car and building firms
B1: a second reason against, e.g. other countries may retaliate / protected firms have less incentive to become efficient
B1: explained with its effect on consumers, firms or the economy
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. justified only short term, against dumping

long.q: Explain two benefits to a multinational company of locating some of its production in another country.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. lower costs of production, such as cheaper labour or land
B1: explained: lower average costs increase profit or allow lower prices
B1: a second benefit, e.g. avoid tariffs and quotas / be closer to customers / access to raw materials / government incentives
B1: explained, e.g. lower transport costs and better knowledge of local tastes, so more sales
